references.text: The preceding context where Jesus teaches the disciples to pray, which leads directly into the parable of the friend who comes at midnight to illustrate the power and perseverance of prayer.
The continuation of the parable where Jesus explains the point: that persistent prayer leads to an answer – "ask, and you will receive; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you".
The parable of the unjust judge and the widow is a parallel story about perseverance in prayer, where Jesus uses a similar argument from the lesser to the greater (kal va-chomer).

Matthew's parallel to Jesus' teaching on asking, seeking, and knocking, with the parable of a father who gives good gifts to his children – the same principle regarding God's willingness to answer prayer.

"Do not say to your neighbor, 'Go and come back tomorrow; I will give it then,' when you have it now." Proverbs emphasizes the duty to help a friend who asks for something, which forms the background for the parable.
Jesus uses a similar rhetorical question form ("Which of you...") to appeal to the common sense of his listeners, here about saving a son or an ox that has fallen into a well on the Sabbath.
Another parable where Jesus uses the same rhetorical introduction "Which of you..." (Τίς ἐξ ὑμῶν) to lead the listeners to an obvious conclusion, here concerning the lost sheep.
